confidence_note: Verified in the archive.org full text, chapter 'Limit Your Inputs'. The story goes back to Emerson's essay on Napoleon; Holiday tells it without page-level sourcing. The old text's 24-hour/one-week waiting exercise is not in the book and was dropped.
facts: As a general, Napoleon made it his habit to delay responding to mail: his secretary was told to wait three weeks before opening any correspondence.
When he finally heard what a letter said, Napoleon loved to note how many supposedly important issues had resolved themselves and needed no reply.
Holiday stresses Napoleon was never negligent in his duties or out of touch with his government or soldiers.
He told messengers never to wake him with good news; bad news, an unfolding crisis, was to be brought immediately: 'Rouse me instantly, for then there is not a moment to be lost.'
Holiday contrasts this with the 'CNN Effect': twenty-four-hour coverage that makes leaders reactive.
His advice: give things a little space, don't consume news in real time, don't let your inbox lord over your life; the important will still be important, the unimportant will show its insignificance.
A century and a half later Eisenhower refused to be handed unopened mail and sorted problems by urgency and importance.
Holiday quotes Epictetus: 'If you wish to improve, be content to appear clueless or stupid in extraneous matters.'
Napoleon accepted being behind on his mail even if it upset some people or he missed some gossip, because trivial problems had to resolve themselves without him.
Eisenhower's insight, as Holiday tells it: much that was happening was urgent but not important, and most of what was truly important was not time-sensitive; this became the 'Eisenhower Box'.
In her 1942 diary Dorothy Day told herself: 'Turn off your radio, put away your daily paper.'

Holiday notes that drowning someone in information is a tactic: lawyers try to bury the other side in paper, intelligence operatives flood the enemy with propaganda; the result is called analysis paralysis.
Holiday's concrete advice: don't consume news in real time, be a season or two behind on the latest trend, don't let your inbox lord over your life.
The story traces back to Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay on Napoleon.
scene_details: letters left unopened for three weeks
messengers told not to wake him for good news
Eisenhower: no unopened mail handed to him
Dorothy Day's 1942 diary: turn off the radio
tension: An emperor at war leaves his letters sealed for three weeks; how does that not end in disaster?
opening_idea: Start with the secretary and the pile of unopened letters, and the three-week rule.

lessons.idea: Sort what reaches you by whether it can wait, and let the rest wait on purpose.
lessons.anchor: Three-week delay plus the instant wake-up rule for bad news.
lessons.example: A shop owner checks supplier emails twice a day but keeps the phone on for the delivery van.

reflect_final: Which message that feels urgent today would you still care about if you read it three weeks from now?

use_cases.situation: Team expects instant replies to every message.
use_cases.move: Propose a rule like Napoleon's: wake me only for bad news; everything else gets a set reply time.
Pick one block for messages and leave notifications off until then.

use_cases.situation: A friend is anxious about an unanswered group chat.
use_cases.move: Mention Napoleon's sealed letters: many issues sorted themselves while he waited.

pocket_idea: Napoleon left letters sealed for three weeks but wanted bad news at once: decide which is which.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Napoleon ordered messengers never to wake him for good news, only bad.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Napoleon's secretary waited three weeks before opening letters; by then many 'urgent' matters had settled. But bad news woke him instantly. Holiday uses it to argue for filtering inputs.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What would happen if you read your messages a day late?
